questions.q: In the context of this lesson, what does a "runaway" agent actually mean?
options: An agent that has become deliberately hostile toward its user
An agent loop that keeps running without making progress — retrying failing calls, cycling between tools, or re-planning the same sub-task without converging
An agent that has exceeded its context window limit and crashed
An agent that refuses to call any tools at all
questions.explain: Runaway doesn't imply malice — it describes a loop that keeps consuming resources and calling tools without reaching a natural stopping point, because nothing guarantees the model recognizes it's stuck.

questions.q: What does Anthropic's own guidance on building agents say is needed to keep an agent loop under control?
options: Stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, enforced externally rather than relying on the model's own judgment to stop itself
A longer system prompt with more detailed instructions is always sufficient on its own
Removing all tools from the agent so it can never loop
Increasing the model's context window size
questions.explain: The guidance explicitly recommends stopping conditions like a maximum iteration count — a hard, code-enforced limit, not just a prompting instruction, because the loop's own judgment isn't a reliable control mechanism.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a "max repeat calls" limit in addition to a max iteration count?
options: It catches a loop retrying the identical tool call with the same input expecting a different result — a common failure that should trigger a stop faster than a general iteration cap would
It replaces the need for a max iteration count entirely
It is only useful for tools that require human approval
It has no distinct purpose from the max wall-clock limit
questions.explain: Max repeat calls targets the narrow, very common case of literally retrying the same failing call — since that pattern is easy to detect, this limit should trip fastest, often after just two identical attempts.

questions.q: What should happen when one of an agent's stopping conditions (iterations, wall-clock time, repeat calls) is triggered?
options: The system should silently discard the session with no record of what happened
The loop should stop, and the system should clearly report what the agent was trying to do, how far it got, and which limit stopped it
The limit should be automatically doubled and the agent should keep running
The agent should immediately retry the entire task from scratch with no limit the second time
questions.explain: A stopped state needs to be at least as legible as a normal completion — silently cutting off a loop with no explanation just produces a confusing, half-finished result instead of protecting the system.

questions.q: How do stopping conditions (iteration/time/repeat limits) relate to the approval checkpoints from Chapter 4?
options: They are redundant with approval checkpoints and only one of the two should be used
They replace the need for approval checkpoints entirely
They address a different failure mode: approval stops one specific risky action, while stopping conditions stop the loop itself from running forever even if every individual action was safe
Stopping conditions only apply to agents that have no approval checkpoints at all
questions.explain: An agent could call only safe, pre-approved tools and still need a hard iteration cap, because the risk of an unbounded loop is unlimited time and cost, independent of whether any single action was risky — both controls run together.
